STEP 1 - Vessel type: flat paper plate (round, white, with a rim band and flat centre, no inner wall visible).

STEP 2 - Vessel size:
a) Type cue: a small paper plate is 15-18 cm; a large paper plate is 22-26 cm.
b) Reference object: the bacon strips are about 15-17 cm long. The plate diameter spans roughly one strip length plus a bit more, so about 1.1-1.3 strip lengths across. Against a 16 cm strip, that gives ~18-20 cm. The plate also looks small relative to the wooden board's width (about 15 cm wide at the board), which supports a small-to-medium plate.
Reconciling the two cues: width ≈ 18 cm.

STEP 3 - Food items:
- Bacon: four to five cooked strips, mostly lying flat, covering about 35% of the plate area.
  - Footprint: 0.785 x 18² = 254 cm²; 35% = 89 cm².
  - Thickness: a cooked bacon strip is about 0.3 cm thick, and strips overlap at one point (about 2 deep), so average ≈ 0.4 cm.
  - Volume: 89 x 0.4 = 36 ml. Bulk density for cooked meat ≈ 1.0 g/ml, but bacon is fatty and lighter once cooked; use 0.8 g/ml → ~29 g.
  - Sanity check: a cooked strip weighs about 8-10 g, so 4 strips ≈ 32-40 g. Taking ~35 g.
- Grease/residue smear: a faint sheen and pinkish smear, roughly 0.3 cm thin over ~20 cm² → ~6 ml → ~5 g of fat.

STEP 4 - Hidden food: none. The bacon sits on the surface with no base layer.

STEP 5 - Energy per 100 g (cooked bacon ≈ 540-560 kcal; the residue is mainly fat, ~800-900 kcal/100 g).

Totals: bacon ≈ 35 g at ~550 kcal/100 g; residual grease ≈ 5 g at ~850 kcal/100 g. Total ≈ 40 g, about 235 kcal.
